meta.title: Who really said "A rose by any other name would smell as sweet"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Shakespeare: Juliet, in Romeo and Juliet 2.2. But he wrote two lines — and the 1599 quarto and 1623 First Folio read "word," not "name."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A rose by any other name would smell as sweet'?
meta.ogDescription: Juliet says it in Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2. "Name" is the 1597 first quarto's reading; the 1599 quarto and the 1623 Folio both print "word."

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1564–1616 · English playwright — the words are Juliet’s, in Romeo and Juliet
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in the primary text: Juliet speaks it in Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2, and the first quarto of 1597 ↗ prints the words “By any other name would smell as sweet.” Two honest caveats travel with it: Shakespeare wrote it as two lines, not one, and the 1599 second quarto and the 1623 First Folio both read “word” where the popular version reads “name.”
answer.confidenceText: Verified in the 1597 quarto — but compressed, and the “name/word” variant is real.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Juliet, at an upstairs window in her father’s orchard

source.excerpt: Tis but thy name that is mine enemie. / Whats Mountague? It is nor hand nor foote, / Nor arme, nor face, nor any other part. / Whats in a name? That which we call a Rose, / By any other name would smell as sweet: / So Romeo would, were he not Romeo cald,
trail: 1591–1595 — Romeo and Juliet is written; Wikipedia ↗ gives this range and notes the play was first published in a quarto in 1597.

1597 — the first quarto, An Excellent Conceited Tragedie of Romeo and Iuliet, is printed in London. Its text of 2.2 reads “Whats in a name? That which we call a Rose, / By any other name would smell as sweet” — the wording the world remembers (Internet Shakespeare Editions, Quarto 1 ↗).

1599 — the second quarto prints the same speech with a different key word: “By any other word would smell as sweete” (Internet Shakespeare Editions, Quarto 2 ↗). The Wikiquote entry ↗ flags the same variant, noting “name” is “word” in the Folio and the quarto of 1609.

1623 — the First Folio keeps “word” (Internet Shakespeare Editions, Folio 1 ↗). Because Q2 rather than Q1 underlies modern editions — as the Folger Shakespeare Library ↗ explains — the Folger’s own text of 2.2 ↗ prints “word,” not “name.”
source.excerptNote: Juliet’s speech as printed in the 1597 first quarto (old-spelling text, Internet Shakespeare Editions ↗). The 1599 second quarto — the basis of nearly every modern edition — runs the middle of the passage differently (“ô be some other name / Belonging to a man”) and ends the line “By any other word would smell as sweete.”

source.rightsNote: Romeo and Juliet was first printed in London in 1597 and again in 1599, so the play’s text — including this line in its original spelling — has long been in the public domain in the United States and is free to quote in full. Only the editorial apparatus of a particular modern edition (its spelling, punctuation, line numbering and notes) can carry a current copyright; Shakespeare’s words cannot.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare (c. 23 April 1564 – 23 April 1616) was an English playwright, poet and actor, and a part-owner of the company that staged his plays. Romeo and Juliet is early work — written between 1591 and 1595, and in print by 1597 — which is precisely why it survives in two markedly different early texts, and why this line survives in two different words. The rose is not Shakespeare speaking in his own voice: it is Juliet, at a window, arguing that a surname is a detachable accident.

cite.sourceCitation: William Shakespeare, An Excellent Conceited Tragedie of Romeo and Iuliet (London: John Danter, 1597), Act 2, Scene 2: “Whats in a name? That which we call a Rose, / By any other name would smell as sweet.” Old-spelling text: Internet Shakespeare Editions, Romeo and Juliet (Quarto 1, 1597), ed. Roger Apfelbaum. The 1599 second quarto, the 1609 quarto and the 1623 First Folio instead read “By any other word would smell as sweete.”

misattribution.heading: Right author, tidied-up line
misattribution.intro: Nobody seriously doubts this one is Shakespeare’s — and that is unusual for a quotation this famous. What has drifted is everything around the attribution: the shape of the sentence, one of its key words, who says it, and where.

items.who: “A rose by any other name would smell as sweet”
items.why: Shakespeare wrote a question and its answer across two lines: “Whats in a name? That which we call a Rose, / By any other name would smell as sweet” (Quarto 1, 1597 ↗). The proverb drops “What’s in a name? That which we call” and flattens the argument into a slogan.

“Name” is the 1597 first-quarto reading. The 1599 second quarto ↗ and the 1623 First Folio ↗ read “word,” and Wikiquote ↗ notes the 1609 quarto does too — so the Folger’s modern text ↗, built on Q2, prints “word.”
It is Juliet’s line, spoken about Romeo’s surname while he stands unseen below and listens — see the Folger text of Act 2, Scene 2 ↗.

Shakespeare put Juliet at a window in the orchard, not on a balcony. Per Mental Floss ↗, citing Merriam-Webster, the earliest known English use of the word — spelled balcone — is 1618, after the play was written and after Shakespeare died in 1616.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Shakespeare, lightly re-tailored in transit: two of Juliet’s lines in Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2, squeezed into one modern proverb, with the 1597 quarto’s “name” standing where the 1599 quarto and the First Folio say “word” (the 1597 text ↗).

context.heading: Why the line survives in two words
lead: Juliet is at an upstairs window in her father’s orchard, alone as far as she knows, working out loud on a problem with no solution: the only thing wrong with Romeo is his surname. Her argument is that a name is a label stuck on the outside of a thing, detachable without loss — hand, foot, arm, face are all real, but “Montague” is not. The rose is her proof. The rest of the play is the counter-argument: the names turn out to be lethal.

There is a quiet irony in the afterlife of the line. The most quoted sentence in English about how little a name matters has itself come down to us under two different words. The 1597 quarto ↗ says “name.” The 1599 quarto ↗ says “word.” Popular memory picked “name,” and scholarly editions largely picked “word.”
context.detailsSummary: The two early texts, and where the familiar version comes from
detailsBody: Romeo and Juliet was first printed as a quarto in 1597 (Q1) and again in 1599 (Q2). The Folger Shakespeare Library ↗ describes Q1 as markedly different from every later early printing — shorter, with a radically different wedding scene — and Q2 as apparently deriving from a different source, which is why Q2 underlies most modern editions, the Folger’s included. Wikipedia ↗ notes Q2 runs roughly 800 lines longer than Q1.

In Q1 the passage is also shorter: Juliet goes “Whats Mountague? It is nor hand nor foote, / Nor arme, nor face, nor any other part” straight into the rose. Q2 replaces that last half-line with “ô be some other name / Belonging to a man” — and then says “word.” Wikipedia’s article on the phrase makes the sharp point that no printing from Shakespeare’s lifetime gives the passage in the form modern readers know ↗, and credits the familiar amalgam of the two texts to the eighteenth-century editor Edmond Malone.
context.pull: The most famous line about how little a name matters survives in two different words.
